sections.h2: How is Kentucky organized when you sell a house here?
sections.html:
Kentucky has 120 counties, and almost every step of a home sale runs through one of them. Wikipedia notes that the state ranks 37th in area yet fourth in number of counties, a legacy of the days when residents needed to ride to the county seat and back in a single day.

That history still matters for sellers. A property tax question goes to the county, a deed is recorded in the county, and a probate case opens in the county. Two big cities blur the lines a little: Louisville sits in Jefferson County and Lexington in Fayette County, and both have their own city guides on this site, Louisville property tax and Lexington property tax.

Below on this page you will find every county we cover, with the cities that have their own page listed under the county they sit in. If your house is in a smaller town, start with the county guide and the county clerk page.

sections.h2: Who do you call about property taxes on a Kentucky house?
sections.html:
Start with two offices in your county: the property valuation administrator (PVA) sets the value and the sheriff collects the bill. The Kentucky Department of Revenue describes the assessment date as January 1, and the owner named on the bill is whoever held the property on that date.

That detail catches sellers off guard. The Department says the current year's bill stays with the January 1 owner unless the sales contract says the buyer takes it on. Most deals split the tax by closing date, so check how your contract words it.

StepWhat the Department of Revenue says
Assessment dateJanuary 1 each year
Real property listing periodJanuary 1 through March 1
Tax roll inspection13 days starting the first Monday in May
Bills due to the sheriffBy September 15
2 percent discount windowSeptember 15 to November 1
Face amount dueNovember 2 to December 31
Penalty5 percent in January, then 10 percent plus a sheriff add on fee after January 31
Transfer to the county clerkClose of business April 15

Many counties mail bills in October or November and then use an alternative schedule with 30 days per stage, so call the sheriff's office for your dates. Our Kentucky property tax guide covers appeals and selling with tax due.

sections.h2: What happens if the property taxes are already delinquent?
sections.html:
Unpaid bills move from the sheriff to the county clerk on April 15 and become certificates of delinquency, with a lien recorded against the property. Interest of 1 percent per month is added, along with clerk and county attorney commissions.

The Department's own example shows how fast it grows. A $1,000 tax bill becomes a $1,254 certificate when it moves to the clerk, and the example reaches $1,704.21 by the June tax sale.

  • The county attorney mails a 30 day notice and, if needed, a second notice within 60 days.
  • The clerk advertises the list at least 30 days but no more than 45 days before the sale.
  • Sales are scheduled between 90 and 135 days after the transfer, which is July 14 through August 28 on a normal schedule.
  • At the sale, a third party can buy the certificate and the lien is assigned to that buyer.

Owners who sell before the sale can usually pay the certificate from the sale proceeds at closing. Ask the county clerk for a payoff figure in writing.

sections.h2: Is foreclosure in Kentucky handled by a court?
sections.html:
Yes. Kentucky mortgage foreclosures go through the courts, and the court orders the property sold. The master commissioner described in KRS Chapter 31A handles the sale, and under KRS 426.522 the commissioner can hire a licensed auctioneer if the lender asks. When the sale is a foreclosure, the auctioneer's fee is capped at 6 percent of the sale price on real property.

The same statute says an auctioneer's sale of real property takes place on the site of the property, so the sale is public.

A judicial process leaves room to sell first. If you have received a foreclosure complaint, a private sale can pay the lender off, and the sooner it closes the fewer court costs and fees pile up. Talk to a Kentucky attorney about the exact deadlines in your case, because we cannot confirm them from the statute pages we reviewed.

sections.h2: How does a deed get recorded, and what is the transfer tax?
sections.html:
Deeds are recorded with the county clerk, and the clerk collects the real estate transfer tax before a deed can be recorded. The Henderson County Clerk's page quotes KRS 142.050: the rate is 50 cents for each $500 of value, and the tax is imposed on the grantor, meaning the seller.

  • The tax is figured on the actual price in the deed.
  • If the deed is a gift or states nominal consideration, the clerk estimates what the property would bring on the open market.
  • The tax is collected once per transaction, in the county where the property, or most of it, sits.

As an illustration, a $200,000 sale has 400 blocks of $500, so the tax comes to $200. Confirm the final figure with your clerk and closing office. For family transfers, our Kentucky quitclaim deed page lays out the exemptions.

sections.h2: What if I inherited the house?
sections.html:
A will has to be admitted to probate in the District Court of the county, and the McCracken County Clerk explains that the probated will and the order naming the executor or administrator are then recorded in the clerk's office.

If the owner died without a will, the clerk's page describes an affidavit of descent or heirship that lists the heirs and the interest each one inherited. These are filed with the clerk of the county where the property sits. A personal representative can also file an affidavit of real property transfer under a will before the estate closes.

  • Fees quoted by one county clerk run from $46 to $50 for these filings, plus $3 for each page over five. Other counties may differ.
  • Ask the district court clerk what proof of authority a buyer or title company will need.
  • Kentucky has an inheritance tax rather than an estate tax, and close relatives are exempt. Our inheritance tax page explains the classes.

Heirs who want to skip repairs and a long listing period often sell the inherited house as is once authority is clear.

sections.h2: What about a Kentucky house with tenants?
sections.html:
Tenants stay in place when a house changes hands unless the lease or the law lets the owner end the tenancy. Kentucky's landlord tenant act sets the notice periods: KRS 383.660 allows termination after 7 days' written notice for unpaid rent and 14 days for other lease violations, and a month to month tenancy ends on 30 days' written notice.

A landlord also cannot shut off utilities or lock a tenant out to force a move. Evictions go through a forcible detainer complaint in District Court.

If you plan to sell a rental, read our eviction process page, the notice rules and the landlord and tenant rights page. A buyer who pays cash can often take the house with the tenant in place, which avoids waiting on a court date.

sections.h2: Does the homestead exemption affect a sale?
sections.html:
It can. The Department of Revenue set the maximum homestead exemption at $49,100 for 2025 and 2026, and it applies to owners who are 65 or older or totally disabled and who live in the home. The exemption belongs to the owner, not the property, so a new owner must apply on their own.

When the title moves, the seller or personal representative must report the transfer to the PVA. Details are on our homestead exemption page. If you owe capital gains tax on the sale, the capital gains page explains where Kentucky's income tax comes in.

sections.h2: What does a cash sale as is look like in Kentucky?
sections.html:
In a cash sale the buyer pays without a mortgage, so there is no lender appraisal or loan approval to wait on, and the house is sold in its current condition. The seller does not paint, patch the roof or clear the yard first.

The closing still follows the same recording rules. The deed goes to the county clerk, the transfer tax is paid, and any tax lien or mortgage is paid from the proceeds. A title company or attorney in the county usually handles those steps.

  • Gather the latest tax bill and any mortgage statement.
  • Tell us about tenants, liens, probate or missing heirs up front.
  • Ask the county clerk for payoff figures on any certificate of delinquency.

Our team reviews each Kentucky house individually, so call or send the address and we will tell you what we see.

faqs.q: How many counties does Kentucky have?
faqs.a: Kentucky has 120 counties. Property tax, deed recording and probate all run through the county, so your county offices are the main contacts for a sale.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Kentucky?
faqs.a: The county sheriff collects the bill. Unpaid bills move to the county clerk after April 15, and the clerk handles the delinquent tax sale.
The tax is imposed on the seller at 50 cents for each $500 of value, and the county clerk collects it before the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Does Kentucky foreclose through the courts?
faqs.a: Yes. A court orders the sale and the master commissioner handles it. A private sale before that date may pay the lender off.

faqs.q: Can I sell an inherited house before probate ends?
faqs.a: Usually a buyer needs proof of who has authority to sign. Ask the county district court clerk and a Kentucky attorney what to present.

faqs.q: Can I sell with a delinquent tax bill?
faqs.a: Yes. Ask the county clerk for a payoff amount, and the balance is normally paid from the sale proceeds at closing.

faqs.q: Will I need to make repairs before a cash sale?
faqs.a: No. A cash sale as is means the house sells in its current condition, with no repairs or cleaning required first.
